title: Keeping an apiary log
subtitle: What to record at each hive visit and why the log pays off.
excerpt: An apiary log is the single most useful piece of kit a beekeeper owns. It holds the last inspection's findings, the queen's state, the colony's temper, and the treatment history. Without it, each spring visit feels like starting from scratch. Here is what to record, in what format, and how to use the log to guide decisions across the season.
sourceNotes: BBKA Bee Craft column, record-keeping features (various issues). Hive Record Keeping, NBU BeeBase guidance. Hive record keeping for beekeepers, Homemade education entry.

glossaryTerms.definition: A written record kept for each hive, noting inspection findings, queen status, colony temper, varroa counts, treatments given, and any notable events across the season.

content.text: An
apiary log

is not a bureaucratic exercise. It is the only way to tell whether a colony is progressing, declining, or showing early signs of a problem. A log written at the hive in pencil on a waterproof card is more useful than a detailed diary written up two days later from memory.
What to record at every inspection
Date and time, and the weather conditions (temperature, wind, overcast or sunny). Colony temper varies with weather, and this anchors later readings.

Queen status: seen (mark with a tick), eggs present, no sign. Note which you actually observed. A tick for 'eggs seen' is more reliable than a tick for 'queen seen' if you are not confident finding her.
Brood pattern: solid, patchy, or scattered. Solid brood on seven or more frames is healthy; patches suggest possible problems.
Number of frames of brood, frames of bees, and honey stores (frames or kilogrammes).
Any queen cells: none, or number, location (face of frame or bottom bar), and whether open or sealed.
Action taken: frames moved, cells removed, treatment placed, feeder added.
What to check next time, with a target date.
The log format that works in the apiary

A single A5 card per hive in a waterproof sleeve, stored in the lid of the tool bag, suits most beekeepers. Each card has a row per visit: date, queen, brood frames, honey frames, temper, cells, action, next date. The card goes back into the lid at the end of the inspection, and the current card is always the one on top.

Digital logs in phone apps work well for beekeepers who can jot notes with a gloved thumb while at the hive. The advantage is that an app can send a reminder for the next inspection date and hold photos of specific frames. The disadvantage is that dropped phones are harder to wipe down with propolis than a laminated card.
Seasonal records beyond the inspection log
Varroa counts: record the date, method (mite board or alcohol wash), and result. Note the treatment given and the week it started.
Feeding: date, type of feed (syrup, fondant, pollen substitute), quantity, and which hive. Useful for tracking how much each colony consumed in winter.
Harvest: date of extraction, frames extracted per hive, weight in kilogrammes, moisture reading. One season's records make it much easier to predict the next.
Swarm events: date, time, whether the swarm was collected, queen status of the parent colony.
Using the log to make decisions

The log earns its keep when you open a hive and cannot remember what you found three weeks ago. A glance at the last entry tells you: what the brood looked like, whether you removed queen cells, and what action was planned. Without that, each inspection is reactive. With it, inspections are a continuation of an ongoing conversation with the colony.

UK law does not require beekeepers to keep apiary records. However, if a notifiable disease such as American foulbrood is confirmed in a neighbouring apiary, APHA will ask for your recent inspection records to assess exposure risk. A log makes this conversation straightforward.
